html:
Kallanai, "stone dam", also called the Grand Anicut, is an ancient weir across the Kaveri river in Tamil Nadu, south India. Tradition credits it to the early Chola king Karikala, around the 2nd century CE. It is still in use, one of the oldest working water works in the world.

It is a low barrier of unshaped stones, over 300 metres long, laid across the sandy river bed where the Kaveri splits into its delta branches. The weir held back the river and sent water into the channels that watered the delta of Thanjavur, the rice bowl of the early Tamil kingdoms and later of the Chola Empire.

In the 19th century the British engineer Arthur Cotton studied it, strengthened it and built a second weir upstream. He used its lessons in larger works such as the barrage across the Godavari. Its success is why "anicut", from the Tamil word for a dam, entered Indian English.

Dating the original structure is hard; it rests mostly on tradition and Sangam poetry about Karikala. Compare the Ganges Canal of the 1850s.
